screens.title: CharacterBody3D: Purpose and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: CharacterBody3D is a physics body designed for direct control by your game logic. It is not fully simulated by forces the way a RigidBody3D is; instead you set a velocity and call move_and_slide(), which moves the body while allowing the physics engine to resolve collisions and sliding. This combination gives you the best of both worlds: precise control for player input and automatic collision handling from Godot. A concrete example is a first-person controller: you read horizontal and vertical input, convert that into a direction vector, set horizontal components of velocity accordingly, and update vertical velocity for gravity and jumping. A common misconception is treating CharacterBody3D like a RigidBody3D — expecting it to react to applied forces. That will lead to unpredictable control. Instead, use RigidBody3D when you want realistic physics interactions like torque and impulses. A practical tip: check is_on_floor() before allowing a jump to avoid double jumps and implement smooth deceleration with move_toward for natural stopping. Reflect: when do you need perfect physical simulation versus direct, script-driven control? CharacterBody3D: Purpose and behavior means it lets you script precise movement while the physics engine still prevents overlaps and handles sliding.. In practical terms, why characterbody3d is the right node for player control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: It lets you script precise movement while the physics engine still prevents overlaps and handles sliding.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › CharacterBody3D
Definition

A node you move by setting velocity in code; collisions are resolved by the physics engine after your movement call.

Key properties
  • velocity: Vector3 representing movement
  • is_on_floor(): detects when grounded
  • move_and_slide(): performs movement with collision handling
Key Takeaway

Use CharacterBody3D when you need precise, script-driven player movement with reliable collision response.

Analogy & Example

Think of CharacterBody3D as a car you steer directly while the road provides friction and prevents you from leaving the pavement. Example: a first-person player where you set velocity.x and velocity.z from input and let move_and_slide() keep the player from clipping into walls.

Common mistake
Trying to simulate physics forces on a CharacterBody3D; it won't behave like a RigidBody3D.
Pro tip
Keep horizontal and vertical motion separate: update velocity.y for gravity and use input for x/z components.
Check your understanding: If your player keeps sliding after input stops, ensure you apply deceleration using move_toward on horizontal velocity components.

screens.title: Implementing move_and_slide() in _physics_process
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the exact movement pattern you'll use in a CharacterBody3D script. The key idea is to update velocity consistently inside _physics_process(delta) so gravity, jumping, and horizontal motion behave the same across machines. You first apply gravity to velocity. y when not grounded. Then check for jump input and set velocity. y to jump_velocity when appropriate. For horizontal movement you read the input vector, transform it by the character's basis to align world movement with facing, and set velocity. x and velocity. z accordingly. If there is no input, gradually decelerate using a move_toward pattern so the player doesn't stop abruptly. Finally call move_and_slide() to execute the movement — this function performs collision resolution and sliding automatically. A common misconception is placing movement code in _process instead of _physics_process; doing so can cause inconsistent physics because _process runs at variable frame rates. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Movement Code
Example script (attach to CharacterBody3D)
# Player.gd for CharacterBody3D
extends CharacterBody3D

@export var speed = 5.0
@export var jump_velocity = 4.5

# Get the gravity from the project settings to be consistent across the game.
var gravity = ProjectSettings.get_setting("physics/3d/default_gravity")

func _physics_process(delta):
    # Add the gravity.
    if not is_on_floor():
        velocity.y -= gravity * delta

    # Handle Jump.
    if Input.is_action_just_pressed("jump") and is_on_floor():
        velocity.y = jump_velocity

    # Get the input direction and handle the movement/deceleration.
    var input_dir = Input.get_vector("move_left", "move_right", "move_forward", "move_backward")
    var direction = (transform.basis * Vector3(input_dir.x, 0, input_dir.y)).normalized()
    if direction:
        velocity.x = direction.x * speed
        velocity.z = direction.z * speed
    else:
        velocity.x = move_toward(velocity.x, 0, speed)
        velocity.z = move_toward(velocity.z, 0, speed)

    move_and_slide()
Explanation & Tips
  • Use ProjectSettings gravity to stay consistent with project physics values.
  • is_on_floor() prevents double jumps by checking grounded state before jumping.
  • Transform input with transform.basis so movement follows player orientation.
  • Decelerate with move_toward to avoid instant stops and make motion feel natural.
Key Takeaway

Place movement code inside _physics_process and let move_and_slide handle collision resolution each physics frame.

screens.title: CollisionShape3D and CollisionPolygon3D
screens.narratorSegment: Collision nodes are the physical boundaries the physics engine uses to determine contact, not the visible mesh. CollisionShape3D holds a shape resource such as BoxShape3D, SphereShape3D, or CapsuleShape3D. These primitives are fast and predictable, so they should be your first choice for character and dynamic object collisions. CollisionPolygon3D or generating collision from a mesh can represent complex static geometry, but they are heavier and may reduce physics performance. A concrete example: use a CapsuleShape3D for a humanoid character because it smoothly slides off corners and approximates a human silhouette without many convex faces. A frequent mistake is forgetting to add any CollisionShape3D to a physics node; the result is a visible object that doesn't block other bodies. Also avoid scaling collision shapes non-uniformly in the editor; scale the parent and adjust the resource parameters instead. Always test collisions by running the scene and nudging the object at different speeds to check for tunneling or clipping. CollisionShape3D and CollisionPolygon3D means keep collision geometry simple and separate from visuals to preserve performance and predictable physics.. In practical terms, how collision geometry defines physical presence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Collision Shapes
Common Shape Resources
  • CapsuleShape3D — great for humanoid players; smooth sliding at edges.
  • BoxShape3D — fast and predictable for crates and platforms.
  • SphereShape3D — ideal for round objects like balls.
If you need highly detailed static collision, consider CollisionPolygon3D or a simplified mesh collider, but profile performance first.
Scenario & Analogy

Imagine wrapping a simple capsule around the player's mesh instead of matching every visual vertex. That capsule is cheaper to collide against and still prevents the player from passing through walls.

Common mistake
Using a high-poly visual mesh directly as collision leads to slow physics and unexpected behavior.
Check
Confirm every physics body has at least one CollisionShape3D child, otherwise collisions won't register.
Key Takeaway

Simpler collision shapes mean faster, more stable physics. Keep visuals and collision separate.

screens.title: CharacterBody3D vs RigidBody3D vs StaticBody3D
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the correct physics node is critical for both performance and behavior. CharacterBody3D is for scripted characters where you control position via velocity and move_and_slide(). It gives predictable movement for players and NPCs that need precise control. RigidBody3D is fully simulated by physics: apply forces, impulses, and torque and the engine computes the result. Rigid bodies are excellent for objects that should respond realistically to collisions, like a rolling ball or a crate pushed by the player. StaticBody3D is an immovable physics body: ideal for floors, walls, and level geometry that other bodies collide against. A concrete example: a rolling barrel should be a RigidBody3D so pushing it causes realistic motion; the floor under it should be a StaticBody3D; the player should be a CharacterBody3D for direct input control. A misconception is using RigidBody3D for the player because it seems realistic — but that makes precise control difficult and often frustrating. Choose by interaction: direct control — CharacterBody3D; full physics — RigidBody3D; immovable — StaticBody3D. CharacterBody3D vs RigidBody3D vs StaticBody3D means match node type to desired interaction: control, simulate, or be static.. In practical terms, choosing the right physics node for your gameplay need. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Area3D: triggers and detection
screens.narratorSegment: Area3D is a detector rather than a mover. Attach a CollisionShape3D to an Area3D and it will report when physics bodies or other areas enter or exit its volume. This is perfect for pickups, triggers, damage zones, or checkpoints — cases where you need to know that something overlapped a region without wanting a physical response like a bounce. For example, make a coin an Area3D that listens for body_entered and checks whether the incoming body is the player, then emit a signal to increment score and queue_free the coin. A common misunderstanding is expecting Area3D to block movement; it doesn't. If you need blocking behavior, use a StaticBody3D with a collision shape. Also note that Area3D can work with collision layers and masks so you only detect the types of bodies you care about. When debugging, visualize the collision shapes in the editor or watch signals in the output to confirm the detection is firing. Area3D: triggers and detection means use area3d for overlap detection and triggers; it does not physically block other bodies.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Area3D
When to use Area3D
  • Pickups and coins that should trigger collection.
  • Zone-based checks, like entering an enemy detection radius.
  • Damage or healing volumes that apply effects without collision response.
Areas rely on signals such as body_entered and area_exited so your game logic can respond to overlaps cleanly.
Example: coin pickup

Create an Area3D with a small CollisionShape3D. Connect body_entered to a script that checks for the player and awards points, then removes the coin. This avoids physics pushes and keeps collection logic separate from collisions used for blocking.

Debug tip
Use collision layers and masks to limit which bodies the Area3D will detect.

screens.narratorSegment: A well-structured scene organizes visual meshes separately from collision and logic. Common composition: a parent Node3D or CharacterBody3D owning a CollisionShape3D and a Camera3D child; visual MeshInstance3D is also a child but does not participate in physics. screens.title: Tunneling and scaling pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Two common physics issues are tunneling and incorrect behavior from non-uniform scaling. Tunneling happens when a fast-moving object moves far enough in one physics step to skip overlap detection with a thin collider. This often affects small or very fast bodies like bullets or thin platforms. Godot offers continuous collision detection options for RigidBody3D and other techniques like widening the collision shape or using raycasts for very fast objects. Non-uniform scaling of physics bodies or their CollisionShape3D resources in the editor can produce unpredictable collisions because the physics solver expects consistent shape parameters. If you need to scale visuals, prefer scaling the MeshInstance3D or the parent Node3D and adjust the collision resource properties directly. A simple test to detect tunneling is to run the scene in slow motion or log collisions with get_slide_collision_count() — if collisions don't appear at high speeds, widen the shape or use continuous detection strategies. Tunneling and scaling pitfalls means watch for tunneling with fast objects and avoid non-uniform scaling of physics bodies; adjust collision shapes or use continuous collision detection as needed.. Tunneling

Occurs when movement per physics frame is larger than the thickness of a collider. Use continuous collision detection or increase shape thickness to mitigate it.

Scaling issues

Avoid non-uniform scale on physics bodies and collision shapes. If you must scale, adjust the collision resource parameters or scale the parent Node3D consistently.

Quick fix
Increase collision thickness or enable continuous collision detection for very fast objects.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn the essential building blocks for moving a player in 3D and making that player interact with the world. We focus on Godot's physics nodes, specifically CharacterBody3D for player-driven movement, CollisionShape3D and CollisionPolygon3D for defining collision boundaries, and Area3D for non-physical detection. You'll see the difference between bodies that are fully simulated by the physics engine and bodies you move directly with code. We will walk through a practical first-person controller example, explain why collision shapes should be simpler than visual meshes, and highlight common pitfalls like missing collision shapes or scaling issues. By finishing this lesson you should be able to implement consistent movement in _physics_process_, use move_and_slide() correctly, and pick the proper physics node for a given gameplay need. Think about your next small level: can your player jump, land, and not clip through walls? That practical check will tell you if your collision setup is correct.

By the end of these exercises you'll be able to implement a player-controlled 3D character, configure collision shapes for efficient collision detection, and select the correct physics body type for different gameplay needs. First, you'll move a CharacterBody3D with predictable results using move_and_slide() inside _physics_process(), ensuring gravity and jumping behave consistently. Second, you'll create CollisionShape3D children and choose simple primitives like CapsuleShape3D, BoxShape3D, or SphereShape3D so collisions are performant. Third, you'll use Area3D to detect overlaps for triggers like pickups or damage zones without simulating physics. Finally, you'll distinguish when to use RigidBody3D for simulated objects and StaticBody3D for level geometry. Each objective includes a small mnemonic so you remember: code for motion, shape for collision, area for detection, body for behaviour. As you practice, check for common mistakes such as missing collision shapes or non-uniform scaling and confirm your character does not fall through the floor.

This second objectives slide focuses on how you'll apply and test the skills. You will set up a test scene with a floor and obstacles, add a CharacterBody3D with a CapsuleShape3D, and attach a script to control movement and jumping. Then you'll create static obstacles with StaticBody3D and BoxShape3D to validate collisions. For detection tasks you'll add an Area3D coin that signals when the player enters, so you practice non-physical triggers. Assessment is practical: run the scene and check that the player cannot pass through walls, can jump and return to floor using is_on_floor(), and that pickups emit signals. You will also inspect common error cases, like forgetting to add CollisionShape3D to a physical body or scaling collision shapes non-uniformly. These applied checks make the learning concrete and prepare you for the hands-on first-person controller exercise later in the chapter.

CharacterBody3D is a physics body designed for direct control by your game logic. It is not fully simulated by forces the way a RigidBody3D is; instead you set a velocity and call move_and_slide(), which moves the body while allowing the physics engine to resolve collisions and sliding. This combination gives you the best of both worlds: precise control for player input and automatic collision handling from Godot. A concrete example is a first-person controller: you read horizontal and vertical input, convert that into a direction vector, set horizontal components of velocity accordingly, and update vertical velocity for gravity and jumping. A common misconception is treating CharacterBody3D like a RigidBody3D — expecting it to react to applied forces. That will lead to unpredictable control. Instead, use RigidBody3D when you want realistic physics interactions like torque and impulses. A practical tip: check is_on_floor() before allowing a jump to avoid double jumps and implement smooth deceleration with move_toward for natural stopping. Reflect: when do you need perfect physical simulation versus direct, script-driven control? CharacterBody3D: Purpose and behavior means it lets you script precise movement while the physics engine still prevents overlaps and handles sliding.. In practical terms, why characterbody3d is the right node for player control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the exact movement pattern you'll use in a CharacterBody3D script. The key idea is to update velocity consistently inside _physics_process(delta) so gravity, jumping, and horizontal motion behave the same across machines. You first apply gravity to velocity. y when not grounded. Then check for jump input and set velocity. y to jump_velocity when appropriate. For horizontal movement you read the input vector, transform it by the character's basis to align world movement with facing, and set velocity. x and velocity. z accordingly. If there is no input, gradually decelerate using a move_toward pattern so the player doesn't stop abruptly. Finally call move_and_slide() to execute the movement — this function performs collision resolution and sliding automatically. A common misconception is placing movement code in _process instead of _physics_process; doing so can cause inconsistent physics because _process runs at variable frame rates. Practice: copy the code into your CharacterBody3D, map input actions, and observe is_on_floor() while you jump and land. Implementing move_and_slide() in _physics_process means apply gravity, handle jump, compute horizontal direction, decelerate when idle, then call move_and_slide() every physics frame.. In practical terms, a practical gdscript example for gravity, jump, and movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Collision nodes are the physical boundaries the physics engine uses to determine contact, not the visible mesh. CollisionShape3D holds a shape resource such as BoxShape3D, SphereShape3D, or CapsuleShape3D. These primitives are fast and predictable, so they should be your first choice for character and dynamic object collisions. CollisionPolygon3D or generating collision from a mesh can represent complex static geometry, but they are heavier and may reduce physics performance. A concrete example: use a CapsuleShape3D for a humanoid character because it smoothly slides off corners and approximates a human silhouette without many convex faces. A frequent mistake is forgetting to add any CollisionShape3D to a physics node; the result is a visible object that doesn't block other bodies. Also avoid scaling collision shapes non-uniformly in the editor; scale the parent and adjust the resource parameters instead. Always test collisions by running the scene and nudging the object at different speeds to check for tunneling or clipping. CollisionShape3D and CollisionPolygon3D means keep collision geometry simple and separate from visuals to preserve performance and predictable physics.. In practical terms, how collision geometry defines physical presence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing the correct physics node is critical for both performance and behavior. CharacterBody3D is for scripted characters where you control position via velocity and move_and_slide(). It gives predictable movement for players and NPCs that need precise control. RigidBody3D is fully simulated by physics: apply forces, impulses, and torque and the engine computes the result. Rigid bodies are excellent for objects that should respond realistically to collisions, like a rolling ball or a crate pushed by the player. StaticBody3D is an immovable physics body: ideal for floors, walls, and level geometry that other bodies collide against. A concrete example: a rolling barrel should be a RigidBody3D so pushing it causes realistic motion; the floor under it should be a StaticBody3D; the player should be a CharacterBody3D for direct input control. A misconception is using RigidBody3D for the player because it seems realistic — but that makes precise control difficult and often frustrating. Choose by interaction: direct control — CharacterBody3D; full physics — RigidBody3D; immovable — StaticBody3D. CharacterBody3D vs RigidBody3D vs StaticBody3D means match node type to desired interaction: control, simulate, or be static.. In practical terms, choosing the right physics node for your gameplay need. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Area3D is a detector rather than a mover. Attach a CollisionShape3D to an Area3D and it will report when physics bodies or other areas enter or exit its volume. Two common physics issues are tunneling and incorrect behavior from non-uniform scaling. Tunneling happens when a fast-moving object moves far enough in one physics step to skip overlap detection with a thin collider. This often affects small or very fast bodies like bullets or thin platforms. Godot offers continuous collision detection options for RigidBody3D and other techniques like widening the collision shape or using raycasts for very fast objects. Non-uniform scaling of physics bodies or their CollisionShape3D resources in the editor can produce unpredictable collisions because the physics solver expects consistent shape parameters. If you need to scale visuals, prefer scaling the MeshInstance3D or the parent Node3D and adjust the collision resource properties directly. Here are the core concepts to keep in mind as you build 3D gameplay. CharacterBody3D is for directly controlled entities where you set velocity and call move_and_slide() to get collision-aware movement without letting physics forces drive the actor. CollisionShape3D is the actual collision boundary the physics engine uses; keep it simple and separate from the visual mesh. RigidBody3D is for objects that should be fully simulated by physics, responding naturally to forces and impulses. Each concept has a distinct role: control, boundary, and simulation. When designing a scene, match the behavior you want to the appropriate node: predictable control uses CharacterBody3D, simulated responses use RigidBody3D, and immovable geometry uses StaticBody3D. Remember these distinctions to avoid unpredictable gameplay when collisions and physics interact.
